The Gate That Took All Afternoon

SYNTHETIC FIXTURE: human-styled text written for tests. Not real content.

I finally fixed the back gate on Saturday. It had been sagging for about two years, ever since the big storm knocked the left post sideways, and every time I walked the dog I had to lift the whole thing with my knee just to get the latch to catch. My neighbor told me it would take twenty minutes. It took most of the afternoon and two trips to the hardware store.

First I had to dig out the old post, which was set in a lump of concrete roughly the size of a microwave. Whoever put it in clearly expected the house to fall down before the fence did. I broke the handle of a borrowed spade on it, which I have not yet told the owner about, and ended up rocking the post back and forth for forty minutes until the ground gave up.

The second trip to the store was for the right hinges. The first ones I bought were for a gate half the weight, and the guy at the counter looked at my photo and laughed in a kind way and walked me to the back aisle where the heavy stuff lives. He said everyone makes that mistake once. I am fairly sure I have made it twice now, on two different gates, about ten years apart.

Setting the new post was the easy part, oddly. Bag of quick concrete, bucket of water, a level held in place with a bungee cord while I went inside for a sandwich. My daughter came out to supervise and asked why the post was wearing a belt. I did not have a good answer, so I told her it was holding its trousers up, and she accepted that and wandered off to look for snails.

Hanging the gate itself needed three hands, so the dog was enlisted, mostly as moral support. I propped the bottom on two paint cans and a paperback, which is not in any manual, and drove the screws in while balancing the drill on my shoulder. The paperback was a thriller I had given up on halfway through, so I felt it was finally doing something useful.

When I swung it shut for the first time the latch clicked on its own, without any knee involved, and I stood there opening and closing it like a kid with a new toy. My neighbor leaned over the fence and asked whether it had taken twenty minutes. I said yes, roughly, and he nodded as if that settled it.

It is not perfect. There is a gap at the top on the hinge side you could slide a letter through, and the paint I had in the shed turned out to be a slightly different green from the rest of the fence, so it looks like it was borrowed from another house. But it closes, it latches, and the dog no longer has to wait while I wrestle with it every morning in my slippers.

The spade, for the record, is still in the shed with its handle taped together. I will confess this weekend. Probably.
